# Thermodynamic behavior of correlated electron-hole fluids in van der Waals heterostructures

Accepted: 20 November 2023

Published online: 13 December 2023

Ruishi Qi <sup>1,2,10</sup>, Andrew Y. Joe <sup>1,2,10</sup> , Zuocheng Zhang <sup>1</sup>, Yongxin Zeng<sup>3</sup>, Tiancheng Zheng<sup>1,4</sup>, Qixin Feng<sup>1,2</sup>, Jingxu Xie <sup>2,5</sup>, Emma Regan <sup>1,2,5</sup>, Zheyu Lu<sup>2,5</sup>, Takashi Taniguchi <sup>6</sup>, Kenji Watanabe <sup>7</sup>, Sefaattin Tongay <sup>8</sup>, Michael F. Crommie <sup>1,2</sup>, Allan H. MacDonald <sup>3</sup> & Feng Wang <sup>1,2,9</sup>

Coupled two-dimensional electron-hole bilayers provide a unique platform to study strongly correlated Bose-Fermi mixtures in condensed matter. Electrons and holes in spatially separated layers can bind to form interlayer excitons, composite Bosons expected to support high-temperature exciton condensates. The interlayer excitons can also interact strongly with excess charge carriers when electron and hole densities are unequal. Here, we use optical spectroscopy to quantitatively probe the local thermodynamic properties of strongly correlated electron-hole <sup>fl</sup>uids in MoSe /hBN/WSe heterostructures. We observe a discontinuity in the electron and hole chemical potentials at matched electron and hole densities, a de<sup>fi</sup>nitive signature of an excitonic insulator ground state. The excitonic insulator is stable up to a Mott density of \~0.8 × 10<sup>12</sup> cm<sup>−2</sup> and has a thermal ionization temperature of \~70 K. The density dependence of the electron, hole, and exciton chemical potentials reveals strong correlation effects across the phase diagram. Compared with a noninteracting uniform charge distribution, the correlation effects lead to signi<sup>fi</sup>cant attractive exciton-exciton and exciton-charge interactions in the electron-hole <sup>fl</sup>uid. Our work highlights the unique quantum behavior that can emerge in strongly correlated electron-hole systems.

Two-dimensional (2D) electron gases have been extensively studied in the last few decades, leading to fascinating discoveries such as the integer and fractional quantum Hall effects and 2D Wigner crystals<sup>1–5</sup>. Electron-hole bilayers<sup>6,7</sup> composed of 2D electron and hole gases that are in close proximity to each other while remaining electrically isolated have been dif<sup>fi</sup>cult to realize experimentally and are therefore much less explored. The strong attractive interactions between elec trons and holes are expected to play a signi<sup>fi</sup>cant role in the thermodynamic behavior of the coupled system. In the limit of low and matched electron and hole densities, the layer-separated electrons and holes can form bound pairs to create interlayer excitons. Interlayer excitons are composite bosons and are therefore an attractive candidate for studying correlated quantum Bosonic states in condensed $\boldsymbol { \mathrm { m a t t e r } ^ { 8 - 1 1 } }$ , whose phase diagrams are expected to include exciton Bose-Einstein condensates $\left( \mathsf { B E C S } \right) ^ { 1 2 - 1 4 }$ <sup>4</sup>, excitonic insulators<sup>15,16</sup>, and exciton crystals<sup>17</sup>. Although these correlated exciton physics can in principle be achieved in bulk materials<sup>18,19</sup>, interlayer excitons in such a bilayer system have unique advantages such as easily tunable energy gap and separate electrical access to the electrons and holes. In the general case of unequal electron and hole densities, the system provides a platform to study a tunable mixture of equilibrium Fermi and Bose gases that contain charge-exciton complexes.

Previous studies of correlated excitonic phases have focused on bilayer systems with semiconductor double quantum wel $\mathbf { l } s ^ { 2 0 - 2 2 }$ and graphene bilayers<sup>23,24</sup>. However, in these systems the exciton binding energy is relatively weak (a few meV or less), so it usually requires a strong magnetic <sup>fi</sup>eld to form quasi-electrons/holes in the Landau levels or requires a low temperature for exciton formation. Semiconducting transition metal dichalcogenide (TMD) heterostructures, due to their strong Coulomb interaction and large exciton binding energies (hundreds of meV)<sup>25–27</sup>, provide a model system to explore correlated 2D electron-hole (e-h) <sup>fl</sup>uids in the strong coupling regime. By inserting a thin tunnel barrier such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) between two TMD layers, ultralong exciton lifetimes, high exciton density, and equilibrium e-h and exciton <sup>fl</sup>uids can be realized<sup>15,28</sup>. Theoretical studies of such heterostructures have predicted record-high BEC critical temperatures with the tunability to explore strong and weak coupling regimes<sup>6,13,29,30</sup>. Recently, electrical capacitance measurements have been employed to probe interlayer excitons in $\mathsf { M o S e } _ { 2 } / \mathsf { h B N } / \mathsf { W S e } _ { 2 }$ heterostructures and revealed the presence of correlated excitonic insulators<sup>15</sup>, de<sup>fi</sup>ned as a chargeincompressible but exciton-compressible state. However, thermodynamic behavior of the e-h <sup>fl</sup>uid across the electron and hole doped phase diagram has not been established.

Here, we develop quantitative optical spectroscopy to accurately determine the local electron and hole density and use it to determine the thermodynamic behavior of correlated e-h <sup>fl</sup>uids. It is well known that optical resonances in TMD layers depend sensitively on the carrier density due to their enhanced light-matter and Coulomb interactions<sup>31,32</sup>. With careful in-situ calibration of this dependence, we can determine the electron, hole, and exciton densities, and then the electron, hole, and exciton chemical potentials of our gated TMD heterostructures. We observe electrically tunable and highly correlated excitons and exciton-charge complexes in this system: (1) An excitonic insulator ground state can appear at equal electron and hole density, which features strong exciton-exciton correlation. The exciton insulator ionizes at both increased exciton density (Mott transition) and elevated temperature (thermal melting). (2) The interlayer excitons interact strongly with additional electrons or holes, leading to an exciton-density dependent charge chemical potential for a <sup>fi</sup>xed net charge density.

## Results

Figure 1a shows a schematic cross-section and electrical circuit representation of our device. We use MoSe and ${ \sf W S e } _ { 2 }$ as the active electron and hole layers and separate them by a 3 nm thin hBN layer. The heterostructure is encapsulated with dielectric hBN and graphite top $( V _ { \mathrm { T G } } )$ and bottom $( V _ { \mathrm { B G } } )$ gates. To create reliable electrical contacts, we follow ref. 15 to incorporate a thicker hBN spacer between the TMD layers in part of the heterostructure (region 0). The TMD layers are then contacted by few-layer graphene in region 0. The vertical electric <sup>fi</sup>eld generated by $V _ { \Delta } \equiv V _ { \mathrm { T G } } - V _ { \mathrm { B G } }$ can control the electric potential difference between the MoSe and WSe layers. It enables a heavily electron doped MoSe<sub>2</sub> layer and a heavily hole doped WSe<sub>2</sub> layer in region 0, which serve as carrier reservoirs for the area of interest (region 1) (details in Methods and Supplementary Figs. 1, 2). This improved contact method allows simultaneous doping of both electrons and holes in the active region. The combination of the thin hBN layer suppressing interlayer tunneling and ef<sup>fi</sup>cient charge injection from the contacts ensures an equilibrium state and accurate measurements of thermodynamic quantities. An optical image of such a device is shown in Fig. 1b.

We control the band alignment and electron $( n _ { \mathrm { e } } )$ and hole $( n _ { \mathrm { h } } )$ densities in the active region using gate voltages $( V _ { \mathrm { T G } }$ and $V _ { \mathrm { B G } } )$ and the WSe<sub>2</sub> voltage $( V _ { \mathfrak { h } } )$ while grounding the MoSe<sub>2</sub> layer $( V _ { \mathrm { e } } = 0 )$ . The interlayer bias voltage $V _ { \mathrm { { B } } } \equiv V _ { \mathrm { { h } } } - V _ { \mathrm { { e } } }$ and vertical electric <sup>fi</sup>eld $V _ { \Delta }$ both create an energy difference in the two layers and tune the effective band gap. The gate voltage $V _ { \mathrm { G } } \equiv V _ { \mathrm { T G } } + V _ { \mathrm { B G } }$ tunes the Fermi level and controls the net charge $n _ { \mathrm { e } } - n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ in the e-h system. We can achieve reliable electrical control in multiple devices and the data shown below is highly reproducible (Supplementary Figs. 1, 3 and 4). Unless otherwise speci<sup>fi</sup>ed, the results below are from device D1 at $V _ { \Delta } = 1 1 ~ \mathrm { V }$ at sample temperature T = 2.5 K.

We use optical spectroscopy to quantitatively determine the electron and hole densities in ${ \sf M o S e } _ { 2 }$ and ${ \sf W S e } _ { 2 }$ layers, respectively. In Fig. 1c, we <sup>fi</sup>rst show representative re<sup>fl</sup>ection spectra R as a function of the applied gate voltage $V _ { \mathrm { G } }$ in the low $V _ { \mathrm { B } }$ regime where the type-II band gap is not closed. When the Fermi level is tuned into the gap and both layers are undoped (middle region of Fig. 1c), we observe strong resonances at 719 nm and 754 nm, which are attributed to the intralayer excitonic responses in the ${ \sf W S e } _ { 2 }$ and $\mathrm { M o S e } _ { 2 } ,$ respectively. When the TMD is doped with holes or electrons (left and right regions), threeparticle bound states commonly known as trions will form, giving rise to an additional absorption peak at longer wavelength<sup>31,33</sup>. With increasing doping, the trion peak becomes stronger, while the exciton peak blueshifts and loses its oscillator strength due to Pauli blocking<sup>32</sup>.

Thus, the re<sup>fl</sup>ection spectrum provides a sensitive probe for the carrier density in each layer. In the well-understood single layer doped regime, the undoped TMD layer simply acts as a passive dielectric layer, and the doping density in the active TMD layer can be calculated from a simple parallel capacitor model (details in Methods). This allows us to create a map between the re<sup>fl</sup>ection spectra and carrier density for each layer (Supplementary Fig. 5 and faded colored lines in Fig. 1d).

When the bandgap is closed by a large $V _ { \mathrm { B } } ,$ both layers become doped, forming a correlated e-h <sup>fl</sup>uid. The black dots in Fig. 1d show a representative spectrum, where trion peaks in both layers appear in this regime. The faded lines in Fig. 1d show the single-layer spectra for electron and hole densities from $0 \mathrm { ~ - ~ } 2 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ taken from the spectrum-density maps. We match the measured re<sup>fl</sup>ection spectrum with the single-layer spectrum-density maps, allowing us to extract the electron and hole densities in this less-understood e-h <sup>fl</sup>uid regime. The solid lines display the matched single-layer spectra, which give $n _ { \mathrm { e } } { = } 1 . 1 1 { \times } 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } ~ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ and $n _ { \mathrm { h } } = 0 . 7 1 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ This spectrummatching method assumes that the intralayer exciton/trion states do not get signi<sup>fi</sup>cantly perturbed by the existence of charges in the other TMD layer. The intralayer excitons and trions are both tightly bound particles with a typical size of only \~1 nm<sup>34–37</sup>, and their optical transitions are only minimally affected by charged particles in the other TMD layer that is 3 nm away. In our experiment, the excellent match in wavelength, intensity and line shape for all peaks con<sup>fi</sup>rms that our assumption is valid.

Figure 2a, b shows the gate and bias voltage dependence of the measured electron and hole densities. From the density maps, we can establish the phase diagram of the carrier doping in the MoSe<sub>2</sub>/hBN/ ${ \sf W S e } _ { 2 }$ heterostructure (Fig. 2c). At low $V _ { \mathrm { B } } ,$ the type-II band-aligned heterostructure has a <sup>fi</sup>nite band gap, and the gate voltage can tune the system from charge neutrality (black) to hole-doped (green) or electron doped (red). With increasing bias voltage, the band gap decreases until it closes at a critical $V _ { \mathrm { B } } \approx 0 . 8 2 \mathrm { ~ l ~ }$ . Further increasing $V _ { \mathrm { B } }$ dopes both layers simultaneously (yellow). This is where interlayer exciton formation is expected. Notably, the carrier density contour lines (dash-dotted lines in Fig. 2a, b) are not straight in this regime. Instead, they show kinks near $n _ { \mathrm { e } } \approx n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ indicating that the e-h <sup>fl</sup>uid is strongly correlated.

The voltage dependence of $n _ { \mathrm { e } }$ and $n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ allows us to determine the compressibility of interlayer excitons and charge carriers, independently. Figure 2d shows the exciton compressibility obtained by the partial derivative of exciton density $n _ { \mathrm { x } } = \mathrm { m i n } \left( n _ { \mathrm { e } } , n _ { \mathrm { h } } \right)$ with respect to $V _ { \mathrm { B } } .$ Figure 2e shows the charge compressibility, de<sup>fi</sup>ned as the partial derivative of the net charge $n _ { \mathrm { e } } - n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ with respect to $V _ { \mathrm { G } } .$ Interestingly, we <sup>fi</sup>nd there is a triangle region that extends beyond the exciton doping edge where there is a charge-incompressible, excitoncompressible state. Previous capacitance studies have shown similar results and have identi<sup>fi</sup>ed this state as an excitonic insulator<sup>15</sup>.

Another important consequence of the formation of interlayer excitons is the scaling of the carrier density as a function of the bias voltage at net charge neutrality. In Fig. 2f, we show the bias depen dence of $n _ { \mathrm { x } }$ along the $n _ { \mathrm { e } } \approx n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ line (black dashed line in Fig. 2a, b). Interestingly, we observe a sublinear increase of the exciton density. Fitting the experimental data to a power law scaling $n _ { \mathrm { x } } \propto \Delta V _ { \mathrm { B } } ^ { \eta }$ gives a <sup>fi</sup>tted power of $\eta \approx 0 . 7 6 \pm 0 . 0 2$ (Fig. 2f inset). This scaling power is consistent with previous theoretical studies of strongly correlated dipolar exciton $\mathsf { B E C S } ^ { 1 2 }$ , where quantum Monte Carlo simulations predict that the ground state energy per exciton scales approximately as $n _ { \mathrm { x } } ^ { 1 . 3 6 }$ , i.e., $\eta \approx 1 / 1 . 3 6 \approx 0 . 7 4$

In the non-interacting limit, the electron and hole densities should increase linearly with $V _ { \mathrm { B } }$ as determined by the geometric capacitance (yellow dashed line). The deviation from the linear bias dependence arises from the exciton-exciton interactions. Such interactions can be understood in two different physical pictures. In physical picture I, we can consider the net repulsive dipolar interaction between tightly bound excitons. This repulsion between dipoles causes an energy penalty to generate a high-density exciton <sup>fl</sup>uid. It therefore leads to a sublinear scaling where the compressibility at low exciton density is higher than that at high exciton density. In physical picture II, we consider the exciton compressibility with respect to the “ideal capacitor” model, which assumes homogeneous electron-hole distributions. We <sup>fi</sup>nd that the exciton compressibility approaches the value predicted by the geometric capacitance at high density, but has a signi<sup>fi</sup>cantly enhanced value at low exciton density. It suggests a strongly attractive exciton-exciton interaction at low exciton density if we use the homogeneous distribution as the reference point. In this picture, we can focus on the pure correlation effect by separating out the electrostatic energy associated with uniform electron and hole distributions. The second picture is widely used in the study of correlation effects in electron liquids<sup>38–40</sup>, and it is the only picture that can be readily used to describe the general electron-hole liquid that includes the electron-hole plasma at high density as well as unbalanced electron and hole densities.

To further quantify the thermodynamic behavior of the interlayer excitons and the exciton-charge complexes in the e-h <sup>fl</sup>uid, we adopt the second picture to determine the electron, hole, and exciton chemical potential as a function of the electron and hole densities. Following the theory developed in ref. $^ { 6 , }$ we separate the electrochemical potential into the electric potential ϕ, which contains the electrostatic energy associated with homogeneous charge distributions in an ideal capacitor and is device-geometry dependent, and the chemical potential μ, which contains the correlation effects in the e-h <sup>fl</sup>uids. Here $\epsilon _ { 0 }$ is vacuum permittivity, $\epsilon _ { \mathrm { B N } } = 4 . 2$ is the out-of-plane dielectric constant for hBN (ref. 41), and $t _ { \mathrm { t } } , t _ { \mathrm { m } } , t _ { \mathrm { b } }$ are the top, middle, and bottom hBN thicknesses, respectively. The chemical potentials can then be experimentally determined as a function of $n _ { \mathrm { e } }$ and $n _ { \mathrm { h } } .$ as shown in Fig. 3a, b.

Notably, the electron chemical potential (Fig. 3a) has a discontinuity across the diagonal line $( n _ { \mathrm { e } } = n _ { \mathrm { h } } )$ , which is more prominent at low densities, and disappears above a critical density. The hole chemical potential also shows a similar jump but with opposite sign (Fig. 3b). In Fig. 3c, we show a typical chemical potential linecut at <sup>fi</sup>xed hole doping $n _ { \mathrm { h } } = 0 . 1 5 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 }$ . By <sup>fi</sup>tting it to a linear background plus a step function, we estimate the chemical potential jump $( \Delta \mu _ { \mathrm { e } }$ $\Delta \mu _ { \mathrm { h } } )$ at this density to be +13 meV and −13 meV for the electrons and holes, respectively. This chemical potential discontinuity effectively opens a gap at $n _ { \mathrm { e } } = n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ for single charge injection, leading to a chargeincompressible phase at <sup>fi</sup>nite density. Nevertheless, the exciton chemical potential $\mu _ { \mathrm { x } } = \mu _ { \mathrm { e } } + \mu _ { \mathrm { h } }$ is continuous (Fig. 3d), and therefore excitons are compressible.

The chemical potential jump across net charge neutrality has been theoretically predicted as an indication of a <sup>fi</sup>nite energy gap in the super<sup>fl</sup>uid phase<sup>7</sup>. It is a de<sup>fi</sup>nitive signature of interlayer excitons in the dipolar excitonic insulator. Close to the excitonic insulator phase, the system consists of $n _ { \mathrm { x } } = \mathrm { m i n } \left( n _ { \mathrm { e } } , n _ { \mathrm { h } } \right)$ interlayer excitons and $\left| n _ { \mathrm { e } } - n _ { \mathrm { h } } \right|$ unpaired charges. When $n _ { \mathrm { e } } { < } n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ , adding one more electron to the system creates one interlayer exciton and removes one free hole, gaining an exciton binding energy $\epsilon _ { \mathrm { { b } } } .$ . When $n _ { \mathrm { e } } { > } n _ { \mathrm { h } } ,$ however, adding one electron does not change the number of excitons. Thus, in the lowdensity limit the chemical potential jump at $n _ { \mathrm { e } } = n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ gives the interlayer exciton binding energy.

At higher densities, quantum dissociation of the interlayer exciton is expected after the Mott limit is reached<sup>42</sup>. Figure 3e shows the density dependence of the measured chemical potential jump. The binding energy in the dilute limit, $\epsilon _ { \mathrm { b } } \approx 2 0 \mathrm { m e V } ,$ , is consistent with previous theoretical<sup>29</sup> and experimental studies<sup>15</sup>. The chemical potential jump decreases with density and vanishes above the Mott density $\mathsf { - 0 . 8 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } c m ^ { - 2 } }$ , above which the excitons dissociate, and the system turns into a degenerate electron-hole Fermi gas<sup>29</sup>.

We next examine the general thermodynamic behavior of the correlated e-h <sup>fl</sup>uid across the phase diagram. To provide an approximate framework to understand the behavior, we can parameterize the total energy per unit area of the e-h <sup>fl</sup>uid as

$$
E ( n _ { \mathrm { e } } , n _ { \mathrm { h } } ) = { } - \epsilon _ { \mathrm { b } } n _ { \mathrm { x } } + \frac { \alpha } { 2 } \left( n _ { \mathrm { e } } - n _ { \mathrm { h } } \right) ^ { 2 } + \frac { g } { 2 } n _ { \mathrm { x } } ^ { 2 } + \beta n _ { \mathrm { x } } \lvert n _ { \mathrm { e } } - n _ { \mathrm { h } } \rvert .\tag{ð<sup>3</sup>Þ}
$$

Here $\alpha , \ g ,$ and $\beta$ characterize the charge-charge interaction strength, exciton-exciton interaction strength, and exciton-charge interaction strength, respectively. The electron, hole, and exciton chemical potentials are given by partial derivatives of E with respect to $n _ { \mathrm { e } } , n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ and $n _ { \mathrm { x } }$ respectively, which yield

$$
\mu _ { \mathrm { e } } = \frac { \partial E } { \partial n _ { \mathrm { e } } } = \left\{ \begin{array} { r } { \alpha ( n _ { \mathrm { e } } - n _ { \mathrm { h } } ) + \beta n _ { \mathrm { h } } , ( n _ { \mathrm { e } } > n _ { \mathrm { h } } ) } \\ { \alpha ( n _ { \mathrm { e } } - n _ { \mathrm { h } } ) + \beta n _ { \mathrm { h } } - \epsilon _ { \mathrm { b } } + ( g - 2 \beta ) n _ { \mathrm { e } } , ( n _ { \mathrm { e } } < n _ { \mathrm { h } } ) } \end{array} , \right.\tag{ð<sup>4</sup>Þ}
$$

$$
\mu _ { \mathrm { h } } = { \frac { \partial E } { \partial n _ { \mathrm { h } } } } = { \left\{ \begin{array} { l l } { \displaystyle \alpha ( n _ { \mathrm { h } } - n _ { \mathrm { e } } ) + \beta n _ { \mathrm { e } } , } & { ( n _ { \mathrm { h } } > n _ { \mathrm { e } } ) } \\ { \displaystyle \alpha ( n _ { \mathrm { h } } - n _ { \mathrm { e } } ) + \beta n _ { \mathrm { e } } - \epsilon _ { \mathrm { b } } + ( g - 2 \beta ) n _ { \mathrm { h } } , } & { ( n _ { \mathrm { h } } < n _ { \mathrm { e } } ) } \end{array} \right. } ,\tag{ð<sup>5</sup>Þ}
$$

$$
\mu _ { \mathrm { x } } = \mu _ { \mathrm { e } } + \mu _ { \mathrm { h } } = -  \epsilon _ { \mathrm { b } } + g n _ { \mathrm { x } } + \beta | n _ { \mathrm { e } } - n _ { \mathrm { h } } | .\tag{ð<sup>6</sup>Þ}
$$

Our approximate energy expression gives an empirical linear expansion of the chemical potentials in the low doping regime. In Fig. 3f, we show a linecut of $\mu _ { \mathrm { e } }$ and $\mu _ { \mathrm { h } }$ at zero hole density (corresponding to a linecut along the vertical axis in Fig. 3a, b). The electron chemical potential (red circles in Fig. 3f) decreases strongly with $n _ { \mathrm { e } } ^ { } ,$ This behavior is controlled by the charge-charge interaction α. Fitting the experimental linecut to a polynomial and comparing it to the ansatz electron chemical potential $\mu _ { e } ( n _ { \mathrm { e } } , n _ { \mathrm { h } } = 0 ) = \alpha n _ { \mathrm { e } }$ gives an initial slope of $\alpha = - 6 6 \pm 6 \mathrm { \ m e V } / ( 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ : The negative α is a manifestation of the negative compressibility in low-density electron gases and arises from strong exchange interactions<sup>38</sup>.

In contrast, the hole chemical potential $\mu _ { \mathrm { h } }$ increases signi<sup>fi</sup>cantly with the electron density at zero hole density (green circles in Fig. 3f). This unusual behavior arises from a competition between the chargecharge interaction and the charge-exciton interaction, and it highlights the strong interlayer correlation effects. With interlayer interactions, the addition of the hole can be viewed as simultaneously adding an exciton and removing an electron. It results in the hole chemical potential described by $\mu _ { \mathrm { h } } ( n _ { \mathrm { e } } , n _ { \mathrm { h } } = 0 ) = - \epsilon _ { \mathrm { b } } + ( \beta - \alpha ) n _ { \mathrm { e } }$ : The positive slope in Fig. 3f is determined by $\beta - \alpha ,$ with $\bar { \beta ^ { = } } - 3 5 \pm 6 \mathrm { \ m e V } / ( 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$

Next, we examine the evolution of the exciton chemical potential $\mu _ { x }$ . Figure 3g shows that the exciton chemical potential decreases with the exciton density at $n _ { \mathrm { e } } = n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ (corresponding to a diagonal linecut of Fig. 3d). Under this condition, the exciton chemical potential $\mu _ { \mathrm { x } } = - \epsilon _ { \mathrm { b } } + g n _ { \mathrm { x } } $ . Figure 3g shows that the effective interaction between excitons is strongly attractive with $g = - 7 0 \pm 2 \mathrm { \ m e V } / ( 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ : A negative g is consistent with the physical picture II described above, where the attractive intralayer exchange interaction, in reference to a homogeneous charge distribution, dominates over the repulsive interlayer exchange interaction<sup>6,13</sup>. At higher doping the chemical potential deviates from a linear line, suggesting a positive second order interaction $1 9 \pm 2 \mathrm { \ m e V } / ( 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } ) ^ { 2 }$ as predicted in previous theoretical studies<sup>6</sup>.

Figure 3h further displays the evolution of the exciton chemical potential with the net charge density $n _ { \mathrm { e } } - n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ at <sup>fi</sup>xed exciton density $n _ { \times } = 0 . 0 5 \times 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \ \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } . \mu _ { x }$ has a maximum value at the charge neutral state, and it decreases with either additional electron or hole doping, indicating an attractive interaction between the exciton and charge in the exciton-charge complex. Using the expression $\mu _ { \mathrm { x } } = \mathrm { ~ - ~ } \epsilon _ { \mathrm { b } } + g n _ { \mathrm { x } } + \beta \big | n _ { \mathrm { e } } - n _ { \mathrm { h } } \big |$ , we can deduce an attractive excitoncharge interaction strength $\beta = \mathrm { ~ - } 3 9 \pm 2 ~ \mathrm { m e V } / ( 1 0 ^ { 1 2 } \mathrm { c m } ^ { - 2 } )$ . This value agrees with that value obtained from Fig. 3f.

Although we have focused on only a few special line cuts in Fig. 3f–h, the parameterized chemical potential (Eqs. 4–6) provides a good description of the complete 2D phase diagram of Fig. 3a, b at low exciton and charge density regime. Furthermore, our experimental chemical potential maps can be reproduced semi-quantitatively by our mean-<sup>fi</sup>eld theory calculations (Methods and Supplementary Fig. 6). The mean-<sup>fi</sup>eld calculations clearly predict the chemical potential discontinuity at $n _ { \mathrm { e } } = n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ . They also reproduce the attractive charge-charge, charge-exciton, and exciton-exciton interactions. However, the mean <sup>fi</sup>eld theory overestimates the exciton binding energy and cannot capture the Mott transition due to the lack of screening in the calculation.

Lastly, we investigate the temperature dependence of the chemical potential in the e-h <sup>fl</sup>uid. Figure 4a shows the chemical potential jump at neutrality $( \Delta \mu = ( \Delta \mu _ { \mathrm { e } } - \Delta \mu _ { \mathrm { h } } ) / 2 )$ as a function of density and temperature. With increasing temperature, the magnitude of the discontinuity decreases, suggesting ionization of the interlayer excitons. At the lowest density, we estimate the interlayer excitons ionize around 70 K. Similarly, the Mott density decreases with increasing temperature, which can be qualitatively understood as temperature aiding the exciton ionization. Figure 4b shows the exciton chemical potential change as a function of the exciton density along the $n _ { \mathrm { e } } = n _ { \mathrm { h } }$ condition (similar to Fig. 3g) for various temperatures. We <sup>fi</sup>nd that the exciton-exciton interaction strength remains constant until \~40 K and then becomes weaker with increasing temperature (Fig. 4b inset). In Fig. 4c, we show linecuts of $\mu _ { \mathrm { x } }$ at constant $n _ { \mathrm { x } }$ (similar to Fig. 3h) for various temperatures. The cusp at charge neutrality becomes broader with increasing temperature, indi cating reduced exciton-charge interaction strength. The <sup>fi</sup>tted $\beta$ also remains constant up to \~40 K and then weakens (Fig. 4c inset). The change in $\pmb { g }$ and $\beta$ occurs before the disappearance of the chemical potential jump, implying a change in the interaction behavior of the exciton-charge complex before the complete thermal ionization of the interlayer excitons.

In summary, we have reported quantitative thermodynamic measurements of a strongly coupled electron-hole bilayer system. The chemical potential discontinuity provides unambiguous evidence of the dipolar excitonic insulator state. Attractive exciton-exciton and exciton-charge interactions are observed for the <sup>fi</sup>rst time. Our work opens many exciting directions for future studies of interlayer excitons and the search for the exciton condensate at higher temperatures without magnetic <sup>fi</sup>elds. The measurements of the chemical potential and interaction strengths allow direct connection to several theoretical predictions<sup>6,12,13,29,43</sup> and serve as a guide for future studies on the interactions in the electron-hole <sup>fl</sup>uids and possible exciton condensates. The technique demonstrated here achieves optical readout of carrier density and chemical potential and can be easily generalized to study other correlated 2D electron systems.

## Electrical contacts and measurements

Keithley 2400 or 2450 source meters are used for applying gate and bias voltages and monitoring the leakage current. In all measurements, the leakage current is kept below 5 pA to make sure the system is in equilibrium with the electrodes. The interlayer leakage current gives a lower bound of the exciton recombination lifetime τ. We assume all the interlayer leakage is from electron-hole recombination in the active area, and the lifetime can be estimated as $\tau { = } e n _ { \mathrm { x } } A / I ,$ where A ≈ 136 μm<sup>2</sup> is the region 1 heterostructure area and I is the leakage current. As shown in Supplementary Fig. 2, the average lifetime \~320 ms is orders of magnitude longer than charge injection time from the contact, which is on the millisecond time scale.

To make good contacts to the TMD layers and achieve equilibrium states, a thick hBN layer (20-30 nm) is inserted between the TMD layers in the contact region (region 0). The vertical electric <sup>fi</sup>eld $V _ { \Delta }$ creates a much larger voltage difference in region 0 than in region 1, so the band gap in region 0 will be easily closed. Thus, for the voltage range we are interested in, region 0 sustains high doping in both layers and forms better electrical contact to the graphite electrodes. Supplementary Fig. 2c, d shows the doping phase diagram for region 0 and region 1 at constant bias volage $V _ { \mathrm { B } } = 1$ V. The scan is performed in a “snake” order, i.e., columns have alternating scan directions. We observe hysteresis in region 0 doping, suggesting that the contact is not effective and has a long response time at low doping levels. In region 1, when region 0 is not heavily doped, we observe hysteresis; but when region 0 has strong electron and hole doping (dashed box), the contact resistance reduces signi<sup>fi</sup>cantly, resulting in a clean phase diagram with no hysteresis. The data shown in the main text is at $V _ { \Delta } = 1 1 \mathrm { \Delta V } _ { \therefore }$ , where region 0 is at a very high doping level. It is also taken as a “snake” scan, and we do not observe any hysteresis down to mV level, indicating our system is in equilibrium with the contact.

## Calibration of hBN thickness

The dielectric hBN (\~20 nm) thickness is determined by optical contrast calibrated by atomic force microscopy (AFM). We perform AFM thickness measurement and optical microscope imaging for tens of hBN <sup>fl</sup>akes ranging from 1 to 70 nm. The AFM is operated in contact mode to get accurate thickness values. The optical microscope images are taken with a colored camera with <sup>fi</sup>xed color temperature and ISO settings. The RGB optical contrast of the hBN <sup>fl</sup>ake, de<sup>fi</sup>ned as (hBN – substrate)/substrate for the red, green, and blue channels of the image, is shown in Supplementary Fig. 7a. We <sup>fi</sup>t the RGB contrast to a $4 ^ { \mathrm { t h } }$ order polynomial. The measured data points and the <sup>fi</sup>tted curve agree nicely with theoretically calculated re<sup>fl</sup>ectivity using Fresnel equations (Supplementary Fig. 7b). Then the thickness of a given hBN <sup>fl</sup>ake can be determined by matching its optical contrast with the <sup>fi</sup>tted curve. For \~ 20 nm thick hBN <sup>fl</sup>akes, the accuracy is typically within 1 nm. For the thin hBN spacers, the relative error of this method will be worse, so we accurately determine their thickness from re<sup>fl</sup>ection measurements of the fabricated heterostructure. We keep the system net charge neutral while scanning the $V _ { \mathrm { B } }$ and $V _ { \Delta } .$ The exciton gap is closed when

$$
E _ { \mathrm { g } } - e V _ { \mathrm { B } } - \frac { e t _ { \mathrm { m } } } { t _ { \mathrm { t } } + t _ { \mathrm { m } } + t _ { \mathrm { b } } } V _ { \Delta } = 0 ,\tag{ð<sup>7</sup>Þ}
$$

where $E _ { \mathrm { g } }$ is the band gap energy. The slope of the gap-closing boundary gives the ratio of interlayer distance to total hBN thickness. Supplementary Fig. 7c shows a line <sup>fi</sup>t of the gap-closing boundary for D1, which gives $t _ { \mathrm { m } } = 3 . 0 \pm 0 . 2$ nm (interpreted as the effective interlayer distance, which is slightly larger than the thin hBN thickness due to <sup>fi</sup>nite TMD layer thickness), consistent with the value determined from optical contrast (2.7 ± 0.6 nm).

## Optical measurements

The optical measurements are performed in an optical cryostat (Quantum Design, OptiCool) with a temperature down to 2 K (nominal). We use a supercontinuum laser (Fianium Femtopower 1060 Supercontinuum Laser) as the light source for the re<sup>fl</sup>ection spectroscopy. The laser is focused on the sample by a 20× Mitutoyo objective with \~1.5 μm beam size. A small beam size provides a local probe that we can park in a clean region free of bubbles. We choose a very low incident laser power (on the order of 10 nW) to minimize photodoping effects. The spectra are independent of the incident light power up to 200 nW. The re<sup>fl</sup>ected light is collected by a spectrometer (Princeton Instruments PIXIS 256e) with 1000 ms exposure time. To minimize the in<sup>fl</sup>uence of laser <sup>fl</sup>uctuations, another laser beam directly re<sup>fl</sup>ected from a silver mirror is simultaneously collected to normalize the sample re<sup>fl</sup>ection spectra.

## Calibration of carrier density

To build a map between the re<sup>fl</sup>ection spectrum and carrier density, we perform gate voltage scans at low bias voltage and low vertical electric <sup>fi</sup>eld. The gap is not closed, so at most one layer is actively doped and the other layer remains intrinsic. In this regime, the gate dependence of the doping density is well understood and can be described by a parallel capacitor model. Taking the hole layer as an example, Supplementary Fig. 5a shows such a scan. When the chemical potential lies in the bandgap (large positive $ { V _ { \mathrm { G } } } )$ , the hole density remains zero, so the spectrum does not change with $V _ { \mathrm { G } } .$ Upon a critical voltage, the chemical potential is at the valence band edge, and the spectrum starts to change. We <sup>fi</sup>rst determine this critical voltage from gate dependence of $R ( \lambda ) - R _ { \mathrm { i n t r i n s i c } } ( \lambda )$ , where λ denotes wavelength and . . . means vector norm, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 5b. This quantity is a measure of the spectrum change relative to the intrinsic spectrum. We <sup>fi</sup>t the initial increase to a polynomial. The crossing point of this polynomial and the constant baseline gives the critical voltage.

When the gate voltage is further decreased, holes start to <sup>fi</sup>ll the valence band. The hole density is then solved from $\mu _ { \mathrm { h } } ( n _ { \mathrm { h } } ) + e \phi _ { \mathrm { h } } ( n _ { \mathrm { h } } ) = e V _ { \mathrm { h } } - E _ { \mathrm { v } }$ , as shown in Supplementary Fig. 5b. Hartree-Fock theory gives the relation between the chemical potential and density<sup>38</sup>:

$$
\frac { \mathrm { d } \mu _ { \mathrm { h } } } { \mathrm { d } n _ { \mathrm { h } } } = \frac { \pi \hbar ^ { 2 } } { m _ { \mathrm { h } } ^ { * } } - \frac { e ^ { 2 } } { 4 \pi \epsilon _ { 0 } \epsilon _ { \mathrm { h } } } \sqrt { \frac { 2 } { \pi n _ { \mathrm { h } } } } ,\tag{ð<sup>8</sup>Þ}
$$

where \_ is the reduced Planck constant, and $m _ { h } ^ { * }$ is the hole effective mass. The <sup>fi</sup>rst term is the non-interacting kinetic energy, and the second term describes the Coulomb interactions. $\epsilon _ { h } = 5 . 7$ is the effective dielectric constant for the hole layer, which is given by the following procedure: We build a layered dielectric environment according to our device geometry, where the anisotropic dielectric constant of hBN, WSe<sub>2</sub> and MoSe<sub>2</sub> are all considered<sup>44</sup>. The screening from the graphite gates is included by applying Dirichlet boundary condition for the electrostatic potential. A point charge is placed inside the WSe layer, and we numerically solve the Poisson’s equation to get the electric potential as a function of the in-plane distance r to the point charge. This potential is <sup>fi</sup>tted to a 1=r decay to get the effective dielectric constant.

In fact, the quantum capacitance is much larger than the geometrical capacitance in our device geometry. Even if we ignore this intralayer correlation effect, the carrier density calibration only changes by \~10%. Supplementary Fig. 5c displays the WSe re<sup>fl</sup>ection spectrum as a function of hole density. The electron density in the MoSe<sub>2</sub> layer is determined in the same way (Supplementary Fig. 5d). With such density calibration maps, the spectrum-matching gives the electron and hole densities in the e-h regime, which is then used to determine the chemical potentials. We check the self-consistency by comparing the determined $\mu _ { \mathrm { h } } ( n _ { \mathrm { h } } , n _ { \mathrm { e } } = 0 )$ to Eq. (8) and estimate the typical error (standard deviation) of the experimentally determined chemical potential to be 4 meV.
